research_topic: Developer Graph Technology Foundation — Identity, Authorization, Collaboration, and Protocol Architecture for ADR 0017
transcript_summary: Deep web research on identity and collaboration technologies for ADR 0017 Developer Graph architecture, conducted June 2026. Research covered AT Protocol (Bluesky) 2026 state, W3C DID v1.1 standardization, UCAN spec maturity and migration path, Yjs/CRDT ecosystem and Rust rewrite, event sourcing and CQRS patterns with PGlite, GitHub OAuth to DID identity bootstrap patterns, and Nostr/ActivityPub vs AT Protocol social graph comparison. The research validates all major technology choices in ADR 0017 and provides deeper evidence for each.

research_findings.title: AT Protocol (Bluesky) — 2026 State, Sync 1.1, Rust Rewrite
research_findings.finding: The AT Protocol is a federated protocol for large-scale social applications with three core services: Personal Data Servers (PDS), Relays (formerly BGS), and App Views. As of 2026, Bluesky has 43M+ users. The relay firehose handles 2,000+ events/sec. Sync 1.1 update (April 2025) lowered full-network relay cost to $20-30/mo. Active Rust rewrite underway with atproto-space and atproto-pds crates. New 'Spaces' concept — authorization and synchronization boundaries for permissioned records. The protocol uses signed data repositories (Merkle Search Trees, IPLD dag-cbor, CID hashes), Lexicon schemas for global interoperability, XRPC (HTTP-with-conventions) for APIs, and event streams via WebSockets. PDS uses SQLite + Litestream. Architecture separates speech (PDS) from reach (Relays/App Views). Key developments in 2026: subscriptions monetization, private state, topic-based communities. IETF standardization ongoing. Validates ADR 017's decision to use AT Protocol DIDs for portable identity — proven at tens-of-millions scale, with active IETF standardization and a vibrant OSS community.

research_findings.title: DIDs (Decentralized Identifiers) — W3C v1.1 Candidate Rec, eIDAS 2.0, 45M+ Active
research_findings.finding: W3C DID v1.1 reached Candidate Recommendation Snapshot status as of April 2026, advancing toward full Recommendation. 45M+ active DIDs across major chains with 15% monthly growth. DID market projected at $7.4B in 2026 (50%+ CAGR). Key drivers: EU eIDAS 2.0 mandating decentralized identity wallets from Jan 2026, Verifiable Credentials reaching 28M issued in Q1 2026 (340% YoY increase), BBS+ signature standard enabling privacy-preserving batch credential presentation. DID methods: did:web — high adoption among corporate issuers (low cost, DNS trust roots); did:key — established for key-only use cases; did:plc — Bluesky's method for portable identity with rotation keys. AT Protocol supports did:plc (rotation keys enable PDS migration) and did:web (simple, domain-tied). The DID document includes signing key, rotation keys, service endpoint (PDS URL). Validates ADR 017's choice of did:plc and did:web as the identity substrate — proven at scale, standardizing, with regulatory tailwinds from eIDAS 2.0 mandating decentralized identity across the EU.

research_findings.title: UCAN (User Controlled Authorization Networks) — v1.0.0-rc.1 Spec, Maturity, Migration Path
research_findings.finding: UCAN spec v1.0.0-rc.1 with 280+ stars, 22 open issues. Spec is complete with four sub-specifications: Delegation, Invocation, Revocation, Promise. Core model: trustless, local-first, distributed authorization using public-key-verifiable capability chains. Principals identified by DIDs. Key properties: self-certifying delegation (sharing authority without sharing keys), cryptographically verifiable proof chains, provenance log, fine-grained capability scoping (custom constraints, time limits), composability (chains for complex flows), offline verification. Lifecycle: Delegation (pass/attenuate authority), Invocation (exercise authority), Promise (await results across invocations), Revocation (break delegation chain). Security: UCANs do NOT provide confinement — delegatees can sub-delegate without alerting delegator. Principle of least authority recommended. Revocation as last resort. UCAN improves on SPKI/SDSI for web/native contexts. Editors: Brooklyn Zelenka (Witchcraft). Authors include Bluesky (Daniel Holmgren) and Protocol Labs (Irakli Gozalishvili). Available libraries: JavaScript, Rust, Go. Maturity assessment: spec stable; tooling emerging but less mature than OAuth; production use in IPFS/Filecoin ecosystem (Storacha), some Bluesky internal auth. ADR 017's OAuth-first + UCAN-compatible shape is pragmatic and validated.

research_findings.title: Yjs (CRDT) — 2026 Ecosystem, Yrs Rust Rewrite, Liveblocks/PartyKit, Automerge Comparison
research_findings.finding: Yjs is the production-default CRDT with ~920K weekly downloads, 17K GitHub stars. Architecture: YATA algorithm (linked list of operations), deterministic ordering by client IDs (53-bit unsigned integers). Network-agnostic (WebSocket, WebRTC, Dat, IPFS). Editor bindings: ProseMirror, Tiptap, CodeMirror, Monaco, Quill, Lexical. Persistence: IndexedDB, Redis. Bundle: ~18KB gzipped (pure JS, no WASM). Yrs (Rust port) is actively developed — aligning with Yjs v14, introducing time-machine API, experimenting with efficient internal data structures. 2026 ecosystem providers: Liveblocks (@liveblocks/yjs — managed WebSocket + persistence + awareness), PartyKit (y-partykit — acquired by Cloudflare April 2024, edge-based Durable Objects). Automerge (~85K weekly downloads): Git-like full document history, DAG of changes, Rust+WASM, startup time ~10s/200MB for 100-page doc (improved in 2.0). Automerge better for version-history-first apps. Yjs better for performance-sensitive real-time editing. Loro (Rust newcomer) best raw performance but youngest ecosystem. Verdict: Yjs is correct choice for sandbox collaboration — mature, lightweight, network-agnostic. Yrs for Rust integration path.

research_findings.title: Event Sourcing + CQRS — PGlite Event Tables, JSONL Export, Projection Patterns
research_findings.finding: Event Sourcing with CQRS remains a prevalent 2026 pattern for auditable, replayable systems. PostgreSQL jsonb is optimal for event stores. Canonical schema: id (BIGSERIAL), aggregate_id (UUID), aggregate_type (VARCHAR), event_type (VARCHAR), event_version (INTEGER), payload (JSONB), metadata (JSONB), created_at (TIMESTAMPTZ). Indexes on aggregate_id, event_type, created_at, GIN on jsonb. Snapshotting optimizes long-lived aggregates. JSONL export: PostgreSQL COPY with row_to_json() naturally produces JSONL format. Modern patterns: CloudEvents envelope standardization, schema registries, CDC from existing databases for event emission without legacy code changes. ADR 017's event table design (monotonic sequence, actor DID, object key, event type, timestamp, payload JSON, hash, previous hash) matches established practice. Feeds as projections derived by replay. Projections cached in Valkey. The dual-write pattern (PGlite first, then Valkey notification) is standard ES practice.

research_findings.title: GitHub OAuth to DID Mapping — Identity Bootstrap Strategy
research_findings.finding: Identity bootstrap from existing developer identity (GitHub via OAuth/OIDC) to DID is a known pattern. GitHub OAuth provides the developer's existing account as a root of trust. The flow: 1) User authorizes via GitHub OAuth; 2) Application receives access token + user info; 3) Application generates or resolves a DID (did:plc or did:key) linked to the GitHub identity; 4) GitHub acts as the initial verifier. Projects like github-did use GitHub as a DID Document resolution mechanism. Gitcoin Passport aggregates identity stamps from various sources (including GitHub) into verifiable reputation for Sybil resistance. Verifiable Credentials from GitHub could attest to commits, repos, maintainer status. OIDC integration with DIDs via libraries like did-auth-jose. Key challenge: GitHub remains the centralized trust root for bootstrap — the DID becomes independent only after the user rotates keys or adds additional verification methods. This is acceptable as a bootstrap strategy with planned decentralization. ADR 017's approach is validated by existing projects and aligns with the AT Protocol's own PDS migration model.

research_findings.title: Nostr vs ActivityPub vs AT Protocol — Social Graph Architecture Comparison
research_findings.finding: Three distinct approaches to decentralized social networking. Nostr: cryptographic key-pair identity, 'smart client, dumb server' relay model, event-based (JSON), multi-master architecture, follow events per NIP-02, Web of Trust for spam filtering. Highly censorship-resistant but no native account portability (relays are ephemeral). ActivityPub (W3C Rec): server-bound identity (@user@instance), ActivityStreams 2.0 + JSON-LD, server-to-server inbox/outbox delivery via HTTP POST, distributed (not fully decentralized). Account portability is a known weakness — ActivityPods and DID integration being explored. AT Protocol: DID-based portable identity (did:plc, did:web), signed data repositories on PDSes, Relays for indexing/firehose, App Views for aggregation. Account portability is native — users migrate between PDSes without losing identity or graph. ADR 017's architecture: Cell-native envelope protocol as backbone, AT Protocol as optional public-facing adapter (not dependency). Nostr and ActivityPub as additional optional adapters. This is the correct decoupling — the graph protocol does not depend on any public protocol.

research_findings.title: Technology Choice Validation Against 2026 Landscape
research_findings.finding: Comprehensive research validates all major technology choices in ADR 0017. AT Protocol DIDs: proven at 43M+ user scale, IETF standardizing, did:plc rotation keys enable PDS migration. UCAN: spec stable at v1.0.0-rc.1, DID-based principals, SPKI/SDSI lineage, OAuth-first MVP + UCAN-compatible shape is the correct migration path. Yjs: dominant CRDT at 920K weekly downloads, Yrs Rust porting, Liveblocks/PartyKit managed infrastructure. PGlite + event sourcing: canonical pattern for event stores, PostgreSQL jsonb is battle-tested, CQRS projections are well-understood. Identity bootstrap from GitHub OAuth: validated by github-did project and Gitcoin Passport. Decoupled adapter strategy: AT Protocol as optional public adapter, Nostr and ActivityPub as additional optional adapters — correct decoupling prevents core graph dependency on any single public protocol. All choices are well-motivated and current as of mid-2026.

implementation_specs.title: Developer Graph — AT Protocol DID Adapter
implementation_specs.description: Implement the AT Protocol PDS adapter as an optional public-facing protocol adapter for the Developer Graph. The adapter translates between Cell-native envelope events and AT Protocol Lexicon schema operations, enabling Tribunus Cells to participate in the Bluesky Atmosphere (43M+ user network).
acceptance_criteria: Cell-native envelope events can be published as AT Protocol records via the adapter
Incoming AT Protocol firehose events can be ingested as Cell-native events
DID resolution supports both did:plc (with rotation keys) and did:web (DNS-based)
Adapter operates as an optional layer — core graph function without AT Protocol is unaffected
JSONL export format matches AT Protocol record format for interoperability

implementation_patterns.name: PDS Adapter Pattern
implementation_patterns.description: Adapter that translates between internal event format and external AT Protocol Lexicon records. Uses XRPC for API calls and WebSocket for firehose subscription. The adapter is a configurable Cell module, not a hard dependency.

implementation_patterns.name: DID Resolution Pattern
implementation_patterns.description: Decentralized identifier resolution with support for multiple DID methods. Uses a resolver registry pattern for extensibility, with built-in support for did:plc, did:web, and did:key.
